source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

coverage.assignment: Lubbers syllabus VI.C(4)(c–d): Ripeness 763–775 and Primary Jurisdiction 775–783
coverage.status: Abbott and Farmers judicial opinions excerpted; Toilet Goods, Ohio Forestry, Nken and other cases discussed in textbook notes

topics.title: § 11.2.4 — Ripeness: Abbott Laboratories and Toilet Goods (pp. 763–769)
topics.description: Fitness and hardship, final pre-enforcement regulation, Abbott labeling vs Toilet Goods contingent inspection, Fortas dissent.

entries.title: Abbott Labs two-part ripeness test
entries.summary: Ripeness turns on (1) fitness of issues for judicial decision (legal nature, definitive agency decision, benefit of more facts) and (2) hardship of withholding immediate review (compliance costs, penalties, practical and legal effects).
entries.laymanExplanation: Can the judge decide now from a stable record? What serious problem happens if the plaintiff must wait?
entries.legalExplanation: Ripeness avoids abstract policies and undue judicial disruption but permits pre-enforcement review of definitive rules imposing immediate obligations.
entries.examApplication: Analyze each prong independently; compare with APA § 704 finality.
entries.examTrap: A decision can be final and still unripe (Toilet Goods).
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner, 387 U.S. 136 (1967)
entries.summary: Yes. Rule was final, definitive and effective upon publication; legal issue fit for review, and immediate choice between costly compliance and sanctions imposed sufficient hardship. The case remanded for review of legality.
entries.laymanExplanation: Pre-enforcement review ordinarily appropriate for definitive binding regulation presenting fit legal question and immediate substantial compliance/sanction dilemma.
entries.legalExplanation: Statutory construction issue was legal, no further agency factfinding planned. Government's later promise to use only civil rather than criminal enforcement did not negate initial hardship. Pre-enforcement suit alone did not stay rule; agencies may oppose stays or invoke equitable defenses.
entries.examApplication: Compare 'every time' labeling compliance versus merely possible future discretionary inspection; address reviewability versus remedy/stay.
entries.examTrap: Do not claim Court invalidated FDA rule on merits; Supreme Court decided availability/timing of review and remanded.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt in assigned casebook chapter
entries.facts: FDA adopted rule requiring every use of brand name of prescription drug to be accompanied by generic name in labeling and advertisements, after statute required prominent generic names. Manufacturers of about 90% of prescription drugs challenged rule before FDA enforced it. Compliance required relabeling, destroying printed material and expense; disobedience risked civil/criminal penalties.
entries.issue: Is a facial legal challenge to immediately binding FDA labeling regulation ripe for pre-enforcement judicial review?
entries.holding: Yes. Rule was final, definitive and effective upon publication; legal issue fit for review, and immediate choice between costly compliance and sanctions imposed sufficient hardship. The case remanded for review of legality.
entries.reasoning: Statutory construction issue was legal, no further agency factfinding planned. Government's later promise to use only civil rather than criminal enforcement did not negate initial hardship. Pre-enforcement suit alone did not stay rule; agencies may oppose stays or invoke equitable defenses.
entries.rule: Pre-enforcement review ordinarily appropriate for definitive binding regulation presenting fit legal question and immediate substantial compliance/sanction dilemma.

entries.title: Fitness: finality, legal issues, useful factual development
entries.summary: Pure statutory construction challenge to final effective regulation is often fit immediately, whereas uncertainty about how policy will apply may require future facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: A clear legal question doesn't need an enforcement case to become answerable; a vague future possibility may.
entries.legalExplanation: Abbott confronted fully promulgated rule with no further agency hearings, unlike contingent Toilet Goods enforcement.
entries.examApplication: Identify unresolved factual contingencies, need for agency interpretation, and applicability to plaintiff.
entries.examTrap: A purely legal question does not alone always compel finding of ripeness.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Hardship: change conduct now or risk sanction
entries.summary: Compliance burdens and threat of serious legal penalties can satisfy hardship if rule changes day-to-day conduct immediately.
entries.laymanExplanation: Waiting may force company to choose between expensive compliance and breaking a rule it believes invalid.
entries.legalExplanation: Abbott FDA 'every time' requirement required all labels/advertisements revised; sizable cost and commercial consequences.
entries.examApplication: Explain exact coercive effect, amount, timing and available later review.
entries.examTrap: Mere uncertainty over future regulation not always enough.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Toilet Goods Association v. Gardner, 387 U.S. 158 (1967)
entries.summary: FDA rule let agency later inspect color-additive premises and potentially suspend certification after refusal; immediate review unripe because inspection and suspension uncertain and later challenge possible.
entries.laymanExplanation: Unlike Abbey's immediate labeling cost, nothing required additive company to change now.
entries.legalExplanation: Court needed facts of how FDA would apply discretionary rule; no irreparable hardship before specific enforcement.
entries.examApplication: Contrast mandatory FDA labeling with optional inspection and suspension.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Toilet Goods: contingent enforcement and no present coercion
entries.summary: Even final regulation may be unripe if actual application depends on discretionary future inspection and enforcement, no immediate day-to-day change, and postapplication review adequate.
entries.laymanExplanation: A rule saying FDA may someday inspect is different from immediate mandatory label rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Court emphasized need for concrete facts and lack of serious interim harm.
entries.examApplication: Do both prongs; check whether suspension automatically occurs or agency first must exercise choices.
entries.examTrap: Finality is not equal to automatic ripeness.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Fortas dissent about excessive pre-enforcement interference
entries.summary: Justice Fortas opposed broad advance review of FDA labeling rule as inviting powerful industry litigation to delay public health regulation, creating speculative courts supervising policy.
entries.laymanExplanation: Companies might use pre-enforcement lawsuits to stall important safeguards rather than solve concrete disputes.
entries.legalExplanation: Fortas agreed Toilet Goods unripe; criticized balancing private costs too heavily against public health and overuse of injunctive stays.
entries.examApplication: Mention as dissent and policy counterargument.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Pre-enforcement suit does not automatically stay effectiveness
entries.summary: A court's willingness to hear legal challenge does not itself suspend agency rule; judicial interim stay requires separate equitable assessment.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may challenge rule while it still takes effect unless a stay is granted.
entries.legalExplanation: APA § 705 and Abbott discuss discretionary stay and possible harm to agency program; Nken four-factor test in later notes.
entries.examApplication: Separate ripeness from likelihood of interim relief.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume allowed lawsuit means agency rule won't be enforced pending decision.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

topics.title: § 11.2.4 Notes — Rules, Guidance, Finality and Hardship (pp. 769–773)
topics.description: Ohio Forestry, rulemaking ossification, nonbinding guidance ripeness, Aviators practical consequences and circuit contrast.

entries.title: Ordinarily legislative rules with immediate force are ripe for review
entries.summary: Definitive regulations imposing legal effects usually fit early review, especially when Congress provided short challenge window, though there are exceptions.
entries.laymanExplanation: If regulation is already law, plaintiffs should normally be able to test legality before getting fined.
entries.legalExplanation: Cement Kiln notes weak need to analyze hardship if fully legal issue and Congress clearly prefers immediate challenge; Ohio Forestry presents counterexample.
entries.examApplication: Analyze whether legislation creates immediate review opportunity and if no further concrete agency decision needed.
entries.examTrap: Not all legally effective planning documents impose immediate practical consequences.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Ohio Forestry Association v. Sierra Club, 523 U.S. 726 (1998)
entries.summary: Forest management plan permitting possible future clear-cutting held unripe; actual logging required many further site-specific approvals and EIS.
entries.laymanExplanation: The plan did not itself cut trees; court could wait for specific logging location.
entries.legalExplanation: No immediate injury; later site challenges possible; subsequent fact-specific decisions aid review.
entries.examApplication: Compare plan vs final permit ordering actual work.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Guidance document is often unripe or nonfinal
entries.summary: Interpretive statements and general policy guides lack binding force and often do not impose present hardship; courts may require concrete application before review.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency memo without legal compulsion may not be ready for a judge.
entries.legalExplanation: National Park Hospitality found NPS interpretation of Contract Disputes Act nonbinding; group faced only uncertainty rather than concrete compliance burden. Courts differ when guidance is effectively coercive.
entries.examApplication: Identify legal binding effect, actual threat of penalty, certainty of agency view and need for later fact development.
entries.examTrap: A document labeled 'guidance' can have strong practical pressure; labels alone not decisive.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: National Park Hospitality Ass'n v. Department of the Interior, 538 U.S. 803 (2003)
entries.summary: Park Service interpretation that contract disputes statute did not cover concession contracts not ripe as nonbinding and without immediate hardship; Breyer dissent saw ongoing bid uncertainty.
entries.laymanExplanation: A nonbinding position on future contracts wasn't enough for majority.
entries.legalExplanation: Book notes full legislative rule containing statement could satisfy finality but not ripeness.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Aviators for Safe and Fairer Regulation v. FAA, 221 F.3d 222 (1st Cir. 2000)
entries.summary: FAA policy declared pilot 'rest' excludes on-call standby; immediately reviewable because airlines needed to change scheduling or risk penalties including license consequences.
entries.laymanExplanation: Nonbinding policy label did not negate practical enforcement threat.
entries.legalExplanation: Pure legal interpretation and present operational effects made case fit and hard to postpone.
entries.examApplication: Use for practical coercion analysis.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Bennett finality test and circuit split over guidance consequences
entries.summary: D.C. Circuit often views genuinely nonbinding guidance as nonfinal absent legal consequences; other circuits sometimes credit substantial practical effects and treat agency position as consummated.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some courts need an order with legal teeth; others see real coercion enough.
entries.legalExplanation: California Communities Against Toxics/Ass'n of Flight Attendants contrasted with Gill/Aviators; National Mining described doctrine as complex.
entries.examApplication: Separate finality stage from ripeness and state circuit approach; decide whether agency effectively bound staff or regulated party.
entries.examTrap: Do not claim all guidance is unreviewable or that practical effects always qualify as legal effects.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Pre-enforcement review may 'ossify' rulemaking or improve it
entries.summary: Mashaw criticized premature lawsuits prompting enormous records and policy delay, while Seidenfeld defended early review as discipline improving rules and helping regulatory beneficiaries.
entries.laymanExplanation: Early challenges could protect lawfulness or become a tactic to freeze policymaking.
entries.legalExplanation: Policy debate presented as academic perspectives, not legal holdings.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

topics.title: § 11.2.4 Notes — Judicial Stays and Nken Four Factors (pp. 773–775)
topics.description: Stays under APA § 705 and equitable factors; separate stay request from immediate reviewability; Zolt problem.

entries.title: APA § 705: stay of agency action is separate discretionary remedy
entries.summary: Agency may postpone action, and reviewing court may stay effectiveness pending legal challenge where justified; judicial review alone does not pause agency action.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lawsuit and a pause button are two separate things.
entries.legalExplanation: Court balances irreparable private injury against adverse effects on others/public interest. Nken emphasizes stay not a right.
entries.examApplication: Ask if plaintiff seeks stay; analyze stay separately from ripeness/finality.
entries.examTrap: Even where harm irreparable, stays require multiple factors.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Nken / Virginia Petroleum four-factor stay test
entries.summary: (1) strong showing likelihood of success on merits; (2) irreparable injury without stay; (3) substantial injury to others from stay; and (4) public interest.
entries.laymanExplanation: How likely to win? What harm without pause? Who else is hurt by pause? Which course serves public?
entries.legalExplanation: Nken v Holder states four factors; generally tracks preliminary-injunction requirements, though statutory contexts can vary.
entries.examApplication: List all four, discuss evidence and competing harms.
entries.examTrap: No automatic stay based on filing APA appeal or on assertion of high business costs.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418 (2009)
entries.summary: Supreme Court emphasized case management need to hold enforcement pending appeal but that a stay disrupts lawful administrative implementation and is not automatic.
entries.laymanExplanation: Courts use four-factor equitable balance.
entries.legalExplanation: Book distinguishes congressional heightened injunction standard in immigration context and traditional stay test.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Stay harms can be asymmetric
entries.summary: If court refuses stay, plaintiff may suffer irreversible business loss; if it grants stay, public health or enforcement program may be undermined for years.
entries.laymanExplanation: One side wants protection now; government argues public needs rule now.
entries.legalExplanation: Abbott Harlan and Fortas made opposite predictions about how judges would use stays.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

topics.title: § 11.2.5 — Primary Jurisdiction; Farmers Insurance (pp. 775–779)
topics.description: Concurrent original court and agency competence, uniformity/expertise, stay-versus-dismiss, and Farmers full case brief.

entries.title: Primary jurisdiction differs from exhaustion
entries.summary: Primary jurisdiction arises when a claim initially belongs in court but a parallel regulatory agency can decide technical issues first; exhaustion instead applies when claim is initially cognizable by agency and court reviews only later.
entries.laymanExplanation: The judge has power now but may send expert issue to regulator first. Exhaustion means you had to start at regulator.
entries.legalExplanation: Usually disputes among private parties or attorney general rather than agency being defendant; goal is expertise, uniformity and efficiency.
entries.examApplication: Ask who has original authority and whether court should stay case for agency view.
entries.examTrap: Don't call exclusive agency authority 'primary jurisdiction'; there must be concurrent court authority.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Farmers Insurance Exchange v. Superior Court, 826 P.2d 730 (Cal. 1992)
entries.summary: Yes, for count 2 court should stay proceedings and require prior resort to Insurance Commissioner for rate expertise and uniform administration, while monitoring against delay. Count 1 was dismissed because Commissioner had exclusive statutory enforcement authority.
entries.laymanExplanation: When court and agency have overlapping jurisdiction, judge may stay pending agency resolution of technical or uniformity-sensitive issues; exclusive agency jurisdiction requires dismissal of claim court lacks power to hear.
entries.legalExplanation: Uniform treatment of intricate insurance ratemaking and expert record production outweighed cost/delay of prior resort. Primary jurisdiction is flexible, unlike exhaustion: claim originated with court, court retains jurisdiction over remedies the Commissioner cannot grant. Court ordered stay, not outright dismissal, for remaining court claim.
entries.examApplication: Separate count 1 (exclusive agency) from count 2 (concurrent court claim), identify technical 20% baseline and court's retained remedies, delay supervision.
entries.examTrap: Do not say Farmers dismissed all counts or that attorney general failed to exhaust remedies.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Judicial opinion excerpt in assigned casebook chapter
entries.facts: California Attorney General alleged Farmers improperly failed to offer voter-required 20% good-driver auto insurance discounts. Count 1 asserted direct Insurance Code §1861.02, which only Insurance Commissioner had power to enforce. Count 2 asserted separate Unfair Practices Act, judicially enforceable by AG. Farmers argued rate and discount calculation needed agency's expertise.
entries.issue: Where court can hear unfair-practices claim but deciding it requires technically complicated insurance rate determinations, should court retain case or require Insurance Commissioner's primary consideration first?
entries.holding: Yes, for count 2 court should stay proceedings and require prior resort to Insurance Commissioner for rate expertise and uniform administration, while monitoring against delay. Count 1 was dismissed because Commissioner had exclusive statutory enforcement authority.
entries.reasoning: Uniform treatment of intricate insurance ratemaking and expert record production outweighed cost/delay of prior resort. Primary jurisdiction is flexible, unlike exhaustion: claim originated with court, court retains jurisdiction over remedies the Commissioner cannot grant. Court ordered stay, not outright dismissal, for remaining court claim.
entries.rule: When court and agency have overlapping jurisdiction, judge may stay pending agency resolution of technical or uniformity-sensitive issues; exclusive agency jurisdiction requires dismissal of claim court lacks power to hear.

entries.title: Primary jurisdiction promotes uniformity and expert factfinding
entries.summary: Courts defer original determination of technically complex rate, tariff or other regulator-specific issues to agency to avoid inconsistent rulings and use specialist record.
entries.laymanExplanation: Regulator understands industry pricing details better than each court doing calculations independently.
entries.legalExplanation: Abilene found uniform railroad-rate reasonableness needed ICC; Western Pacific technical classification; Merchants handled simple tariff meaning in court; Nader allowed ordinary fraudulent misrepresentation court case.
entries.examApplication: Identify complex factual/discretionary judgment, risk divergent rulings and if agency actually has unique expertise.
entries.examTrap: Purely legal or common-law fraud claims within ordinary judge competence may not justify agency referral.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Texas & Pacific Railway v. Abilene Cotton Oil, 204 U.S. 426 (1907)
entries.summary: Common law shipper's rate reasonableness suit deferred to ICC to ensure nationally uniform railroad rate treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Different courts setting different proper railroad charges would be unworkable.
entries.legalExplanation: Origin of primary jurisdiction doctrine.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Great Northern Railway v. Merchants Elevator, 259 U.S. 285 (1922)
entries.summary: Court could interpret tariff directly because no technical disputed facts or ICC expertise needed.
entries.laymanExplanation: Not every railroad contract question needs regulator first.
entries.legalExplanation: Contrasts Abilene and Western Pacific.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: United States v. Western Pacific Railroad, 352 U.S. 59 (1956)
entries.summary: Whether steel bomb cases containing napalm were incendiary bombs or gasoline in drums for tariffs required technical ICC expertise, so agency-first.
entries.laymanExplanation: Technical classification needed industry facts.
entries.legalExplanation: Even document interpretation may require agency factfinding.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Nader v. Allegheny Airlines, 426 U.S. 290 (1976)
entries.summary: Common-law fraud suit over overbooked airline ticket proceeded in court; regulator lacked special added expertise on familiar fraud standards.
entries.laymanExplanation: Judge can decide ordinary fraud claim without airline regulator.
entries.legalExplanation: No threatened inconsistency with uniform pricing standard.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Stay, dismiss or ask agency for views
entries.summary: When agency can dispose of all issues, court may dismiss or channel whole case; when only some issues require specialist views, court stays and retains case for remaining relief; sometimes receives amicus agency opinion.
entries.laymanExplanation: Court pauses only parts needing regulator then resumes to resolve damages or other remaining claims.
entries.legalExplanation: Farmers stayed court claim to preserve civil penalties even though Commissioner couldn't award those; judge monitors progress.
entries.examApplication: Identify scope of overlapping authority and remedy that only court can grant.
entries.examTrap: A referral does not imply plaintiff lost original court jurisdiction.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

topics.title: § 11.2.5 Notes — Delay, Exclusive Jurisdiction and Private Rights (pp. 779–783)
topics.description: Limits of agency-first referrals, possible private statutory claims, Sandoval and casino Leonard hypothetical.

entries.title: Balancing delay and claimed agency superiority
entries.summary: Primary jurisdiction is flexible: court need not refer simple dispute if agency proceeding would impose major delay outweighing expertise/uniformity value.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sending easy question to an agency for years is a bad use of parties' and court's time.
entries.legalExplanation: National Communications Association v AT&T found predicted 2–5 year FCC delay outweighed benefit for straightforward tariff issue; courts may set referral deadlines like 180 days.
entries.examApplication: Weigh complexity, actual expertise, likely duration and adequate remedy after referral.
entries.examTrap: Do not automatically defer to regulator merely because it has interest in subject matter.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: National Communications Association v. AT&T, 46 F.3d 220 (2d Cir. 1995)
entries.summary: Court rejected FCC referral for relatively simple long-distance reseller tariff question given two-to-five-year delay.
entries.laymanExplanation: Legal straightforwardness plus cost of delay favored court first.
entries.legalExplanation: Context-specific primary jurisdiction decision.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Private right of action logically precedes primary jurisdiction
entries.summary: If statute grants only governmental enforcement and no private right to sue, court cannot use primary jurisdiction to create plaintiff's civil action; decide cause of action first.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lawsuit must legally exist before deciding which forum goes first.
entries.legalExplanation: Book describes shift from generous Borak implied remedies through Cort factors to stricter congressional intent under Sandoval.
entries.examApplication: Check plaintiff's own statute, civil remedy and remedy type before considering agency referral.
entries.examTrap: Don't infer damages suit solely from existence of agency regulation prohibiting conduct.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Implied private rights now demand affirmative congressional intent
entries.summary: Modern federal decisions ordinarily will not infer individual civil action to enforce regulatory rule absent affirmative statutory intent to create both right and remedy.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency regulation saying 'businesses may not do X' doesn't necessarily let customers sue for damages.
entries.legalExplanation: Alexander v Sandoval refused private enforcement of disparate-impact rule under Title VI §602; contrast Cannon's older implied Title IX right and historical Cort v Ash balancing.
entries.examApplication: Identify express cause, statutory text showing Congress intended private remedies, versus rule-created obligations alone.
entries.examTrap: Cort historical four-factor test is not today's default federal approach.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Alexander v. Sandoval, 532 U.S. 275 (2001)
entries.summary: No implied private action to enforce DOJ Title VI disparate impact rule absent intent in Congress's enactment; regulation alone cannot create private remedy.
entries.laymanExplanation: A valid administrative duty doesn't itself create private plaintiff lawsuit.
entries.legalExplanation: Majority emphasized intent; Stevens dissent favored contextual congressional interpretation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)
entries.sourceRole: Case summarized or excerpt quoted in casebook notes; full opinion not assigned in this upload

entries.title: Cort v. Ash four factors as historical framework and state influence
entries.summary: Earlier Cort balancing considered special beneficiary class, legislative intent, consistency with statute, and whether remedy traditionally state-law; modern Supreme Court uses stricter congressional-intent approach.
entries.laymanExplanation: Older courts weighed many practical factors; now text and congressional intent dominate.
entries.legalExplanation: Some states still use Cort-like tests, per chapter. Do not equate with modern federal controlling rule.
entries.examApplication: If state statute, examine jurisdiction and adopted implied-action approach.
entries.examTrap: Citing Cort as binding federal universal test after Sandoval is an exam trap.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

entries.title: Primary jurisdiction and agency exclusive authority are separate
entries.summary: Agency exclusive jurisdiction defeats direct court count; primary jurisdiction refers issue within concurrent authority and usually retains judicial action.
entries.laymanExplanation: If law says only casino commission may hear claim, first ask whether private suit exists at all; 'agency first' cannot fix exclusive court bar.
entries.legalExplanation: Farmers illustrated difference in distinct counts; courts sometimes ask agency amicus rather than formal referral.
entries.examApplication: Check agency statutory text 'exclusive jurisdiction', who can initiate agency case, scope of court claim and remedies.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume casino player's private damages action exists because commission can order restitution.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026)

problems.title: Abbott vs Toilet Goods — opposite outcomes
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 764–768)
problems.prompt: Both challenged formal FDA regulations before enforcement. Explain precisely how fitness, finality, immediate hardship, future discretion and later remedies caused different ripeness outcomes.

problems.prompt: Compare majority's pre-enforcement review rationale with Fortas's concern large firms can stall public-health rules. How does ability to deny stay affect the debate?

problems.title: Ohio Forestry site-specific approvals
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 769–770)
problems.prompt: Why is final forest management plan allowing potential clear-cutting less ripe than binding FDA label rule? Consider intervening site choices and remaining public participation.

problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 771–773)

problems.title: Zolt Chemicals / Hazardous Ranking System — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 774–775)
problems.prompt: EPA issued non-notice-comment 'policy statement' Hazardous Ranking System scoring Superfund site toxicity, release probability and exposed population. The methodology itself designated no sites; Zolt fears future high priority cleanup score and stock-price loss. May Zolt seek immediate review? Analyze finality, fitness, hardship and likely application. If allowed, assess a stay under all four Nken factors. Do not solve.

problems.title: Farmers: count 1 versus count 2
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 775–779)
problems.prompt: Why was Insurance Code count 1 dismissed for exclusive jurisdiction while Unfair Practices Act count 2 stayed for primary jurisdiction? Identify expert ratemaking and court's remaining civil penalties remedy.

problems.title: Leonard / Dusty's Casino — textbook problem
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 783)
problems.prompt: Madison CCC exclusively handles delegated casino regulation, licenses, civil penalties, restitution and proceedings initiated by director; CCC prohibits gambling by intoxicated patrons. Leonard drank 12 free alcoholic drinks, lost $1m blackjack, sued private casino for $1m return and $3m punitive damages. Casino moves to dismiss alleging CCC exclusive or primary jurisdiction. Analyze implied/private cause of action, scope of exclusivity, concurrent court tort/regulatory claims, technical expertise, remedy limits and possible agency referral. Leave unanswered.

problems.title: What if agency cannot award requested court remedy?
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 779–780)
problems.prompt: Agency can decide technical liability but cannot award civil penalties, punitive damages or some judicial remedies. Should court dismiss or stay part of suit? Distinguish Farmers case.

problems.title: Cort versus Sandoval and rights under regulatory rule
problems.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 11, pp. 763–783 (uploaded Nov. 23, 2026) (p. 781–783)
problems.prompt: An administrative regulation bans a particular business practice but statute provides only agency enforcement. Under current federal framework, is there an implied civil right to sue? Compare historic Cort criteria and Sandoval emphasis on Congress.
